```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

#course data (read once for the whole page)
canopy_raster <- rast("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1qxedXO256Xf-dP-rSeE0icQ-Hi-a3ioC")
torn <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1K5yFnDthJGKnWPragZPmQyCDpf8seSEI", quiet = TRUE)

#numbers quoted in the text below come from here, so they stay right if the data changes
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
```

## Part 1: Walkthrough {#walkthrough}

Run each chunk in your own .Rmd. You will reuse this code in Part 2.

### Step 1: Load and Map the Population

::: {.why}
The raster is the percent of tree canopy in each 30-meter pixel around Chapel Hill, from the [2023 National Land Cover Database](https://www.mrlc.gov/data/type/nlcd-tree-canopy-cover). Because we have every pixel, we know the true population mean and standard deviation.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

#tree canopy raster
canopy_raster <- rast("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1qxedXO256Xf-dP-rSeE0icQ-Hi-a3ioC")
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Map of percent tree canopy around Chapel Hill. Most of the area is heavily forested, with low canopy along major roads and in the town centers."}
tm_shape(canopy_raster) +
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(values = "carto.sunset_dark", n = 5))
```

### Step 2: Describe the Population

```{r, fig.alt = "Histogram of percent tree canopy for every pixel. The distribution is far from normal, with large spikes near 0 and near 90 percent."}
#one row per pixel
canopy_df <- as.data.frame(canopy_raster)
names(canopy_df) <- "canopy"

pop_mean <- mean(canopy_df$canopy)
pop_sd <- sd(canopy_df$canopy)

ggplot(canopy_df, aes(x = canopy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Tree canopy (%)", y = "Number of pixels")
```

The population mean is `r fmt(pop_mean)`% and the standard deviation is `r fmt(pop_sd)`%.

### Step 3: Build a Sampling Distribution

::: {.why}
Take many random samples of the same size, and keep the mean of each one. `set.seed()` makes the random draws repeatable, so your numbers match your partner's when you use the same seed.
:::

```{r, fig.alt = "Histogram of 300 sample means with n = 75. The means form a single symmetric, bell-shaped hump centered near the population mean."}
set.seed(391)

#300 samples of 75 pixels each, keeping each sample's mean
sample_means <- replicate(300, mean(sample(canopy_df$canopy, size = 75, replace = TRUE)))
means_df <- data.frame(sample_mean = sample_means)

ggplot(means_df, aes(x = sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Sample mean of tree canopy (%)", y = "Number of samples")
```

### Step 4: Compare the Sampling Distribution with the Population

::: {.why}
The CLT says the mean of the sample means is close to the population mean, and their standard deviation (the standard error) is close to the population standard deviation divided by the square root of n.
:::

```{r}
#center: mean of the sample means vs. the population mean
mean(sample_means)
pop_mean

#spread: standard error from the samples vs. from the formula
sd(sample_means)
pop_sd / sqrt(75)
```

## Part 2: Partner Practice {#partner-practice}

Both partners treat the path lengths of all `r fmt(nrow(torn), 0)` U.S. tornadoes from 1954 to 2022 as the population. The `len` column is the path length in miles. Partner A takes small samples of 5 tornadoes, and Partner B takes larger samples of 50. Each task tells you in parentheses which walkthrough step to reuse.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#tornado touchdown points, 1954-2022 (both partners)
torn <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1K5yFnDthJGKnWPragZPmQyCDpf8seSEI")
torn_len <- torn$len
```

:::: {.partners}
::: {.partner .partner-a}
### Partner A: Samples of 5

1. Find the population mean and standard deviation of `torn_len`, and plot its histogram. *(Step 2)*
2. Run `set.seed(391)`, then take 500 samples of 5 tornadoes and keep each sample's mean. *(Step 3)*
3. Plot a histogram of your 500 sample means. *(Step 3)*
4. Find the mean and standard deviation of your sample means, and the standard error from the formula. *(Step 4)*

When you finish, bring your mean of the sample means, both standard errors and your histogram to Part 3.
:::

::: {.partner .partner-b}
### Partner B: Samples of 50

1. Find the population mean and standard deviation of `torn_len`, and plot its histogram. *(Step 2)*
2. Run `set.seed(391)`, then take 500 samples of 50 tornadoes and keep each sample's mean. *(Step 3)*
3. Plot a histogram of your 500 sample means. *(Step 3)*
4. Find the mean and standard deviation of your sample means, and the standard error from the formula. *(Step 4)*

When you finish, bring your mean of the sample means, both standard errors and your histogram to Part 3.
:::
::::

## Part 3: Together {#together}

1. Fill in the table.
2. Put your two histograms side by side. Which one looks normal, and why doesn't the other one?
3. Partner B's samples are 10 times larger than Partner A's. Work out how many times smaller Partner B's standard error is, and check it against the formula.

| Sample size | Mean of the sample means | Standard error from the samples | Standard error from the formula |
|---|---|---|---|
| n = 5 (Partner A) | | | |
| n = 50 (Partner B) | | | |

::: {.deliver}
Each pair turns in one index card before leaving. Write both of your names on it, fill in the six numbers from the table, and add two or three sentences explaining why the n = 50 histogram looks normal when the tornado lengths themselves are not.
:::

## Answer Key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
torn_len <- torn$len
p_mean <- mean(torn_len); p_sd <- sd(torn_len)
set.seed(391)
means_5 <- replicate(500, mean(sample(torn_len, size = 5, replace = TRUE)))
set.seed(391)
means_50 <- replicate(500, mean(sample(torn_len, size = 50, replace = TRUE)))
```

Population: mean `r fmt(p_mean)` miles, standard deviation `r fmt(p_sd)` miles. With `set.seed(391)` the numbers below match exactly. With another seed they will be close.

| Sample size | Mean of the sample means | Standard error from the samples | Standard error from the formula |
|---|---|---|---|
| n = 5 | `r fmt(mean(means_5))` | `r fmt(sd(means_5))` | `r fmt(p_sd / sqrt(5))` |
| n = 50 | `r fmt(mean(means_50))` | `r fmt(sd(means_50))` | `r fmt(p_sd / sqrt(50))` |

The n = 50 standard error is `r fmt(sd(means_5) / sd(means_50), 1)` times smaller than the n = 5 one. The formula predicts √10, which is about 3.2.

A good card says something like this. Tornado path lengths are very right-skewed, because most tornadoes are short and a few travel more than 100 miles. With samples of 5, one long tornado can pull a sample's mean far to the right, so the sample means are still right-skewed. With samples of 50, those long tornadoes average out, so the sample means pile up symmetrically around the population mean. That is the Central Limit Theorem: the sampling distribution of the mean becomes approximately normal as n grows, even when the population is not normal.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
torn <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1K5yFnDthJGKnWPragZPmQyCDpf8seSEI")
torn_len <- torn$len

#### both partners: the population (Step 2) ####
pop_mean <- mean(torn_len)
pop_sd <- sd(torn_len)

ggplot(data.frame(len = torn_len), aes(x = len)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Path length (miles)", y = "Number of tornadoes")

#### Partner A: samples of 5 ####
set.seed(391)
means_5 <- replicate(500, mean(sample(torn_len, size = 5, replace = TRUE)))

ggplot(data.frame(sample_mean = means_5), aes(x = sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Sample mean path length (miles), n = 5", y = "Number of samples")

mean(means_5)
sd(means_5)
pop_sd / sqrt(5)

#### Partner B: samples of 50 ####
set.seed(391)
means_50 <- replicate(500, mean(sample(torn_len, size = 50, replace = TRUE)))

ggplot(data.frame(sample_mean = means_50), aes(x = sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Sample mean path length (miles), n = 50", y = "Number of samples")

mean(means_50)
sd(means_50)
pop_sd / sqrt(50)

#### Part 3: together ####
sd(means_5) / sd(means_50)
sqrt(10)
```
